newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo businesses urge clearer growth measures.
newsitem.headline: Yugo businesses urge clearer growth measures.

text.p: Yugoslav businessmen on Wednesday backed the government's ambitious 1997 growth plan despite concerns that its targets may be unrealistic without measures to improve the economic environment.
The government has forecast gross domestic product (GDP) will rise 10-13 percent and industrial production by some 10 percent in 1997.
"Global economic policy looks stimulating and it would be a success to achieve the targets. But it seems unrealistic," said Vlada Markovic, general manager of the Merima cosmetics plant.
Members of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce's Economics Department called for more government help in creating a basic environment that would enable solid expansion of the economy.

"It's good the government intends to pursue price and currency stability but it must also provide more export stimulus, liberalise import quotas and do something about banks who charge too much for their scarce credit support," said Miloje Mihajlovic, secretary of the department.
Branislava Zunic of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce said the proposed economic policy paper did not explain how growth targets would be achieved.
Zunic cautioned that due to overestimated growth rates Yugoslavia would once again face economic failure and be unable to meet the targets.
She questioned the need to nominally increase public spending by 32.5 percent to retain its 47.5 percent share in the GDP. "Such an increase means inflationary expectations."
The government economic policy paper says 1997 growth will be export-driven, implying greater industrial output.
Markovic of Merima said an export-oriented economy needed to be cost-effective and responsive with its quality and design to export markets' demands.
Another director cautioned that export orientation failed to bring results in 1996 with trade gap topping $1.7 billion.
"We are all export-oriented, but see no financial results," director of the Jagodina cable factory said.
To raise productivity, achieve cost-effectiveness and improve quality and design, Yugoslav producers needed a lot more working capital to expand business activity, company directors said.
Businessmen agreed they could not rely on bigger support from commercial banks who charge a lot for their scarce credit.

Apart from lack of working capital, Yugoslav companies were oversized for the present (domestic) market, its needs and purchasing power, said Mico Bogdanovic director of the Petar Drapsin metal ware factory. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
